messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 73

On a Wednesday morning in late September, three years ago, he watches the I-beam swing free from the crane. The rigging had been wrong—he knew it, felt it in his gut the moment he saw the angle—but he wasn’t the foreman, so he says nothing. Michael is two stories up on the adjacent scaffold, reaching for a tie-off point, when the load shifts. The snap of the cable is a sound he will hear in his sleep, in the shower, in the quiet moments between hammer blows. He sees Michael’s body hit the rebar cage below. The foreman’s scream is still inside his ears, a low buzz that never fully stops.

After that, he goes back to work the next day. Someone has to finish the pour. He tells himself it’s what any man would do. But his hands shake when he climbs the scaffolding. He checks every shackle, every sling, three times, four times, until the foreman yells at him to move. He starts staying late, just to make sure nothing is left undone, because if the site isn’t perfect, something else will fall. His wife says he’s never home, and when he is, he’s staring at the wall. He doesn’t tell her about the dreams. He doesn’t tell anyone.

The divorce comes eighteen months later. She says he’s not the man she married, and she’s right. He can’t feel her touch the way he used to. When she cries, he feels nothing but a vague irritation, like a stone in his boot. He moves into a studio apartment above a garage, eats takeout, sleeps in his clothes. The only thing that still makes sense is the job site—the noise, the grit, the endless physical push. But even there, he finds himself scanning the sky for falling loads. He listens for the wrong kind of creak in the scaffolding. Once, he walks off a job because a foreman’s voice is too loud, too much like that morning’s scream.

His crew notices. They say he’s jumpy. He snaps at a laborer for standing too close to a trench edge. He refuses to work on the fifteenth floor of a high-rise after a storm. He drives forty minutes out of his way to avoid the exit by the old site. None of this feels strange to him—it feels necessary. He keeps a small bottle of whiskey in his lunchbox. He drinks it in the truck before he goes home, so he can sleep three or four hours before the dream finds him again. In the dream, he’s the one on the beam, and the cable snaps, and he falls, but he never hits the ground. He always wakes up right before impact, heart slamming, the sheets soaked.

He doesn’t talk about Michael. Not to the counselor his ex-wife made him see, not to the union rep who asked if he was okay. He says he’s fine. He says it was an accident. But at night, alone in the studio, he replays the rigging angle over and over, wondering if he could have said something different. He still works, because what else is there. But every morning he finds his palms sweating before he even opens the truck door. He checks his harness three times. He stands with his back to the wall whenever he can. And he waits for the next thing to fall.
